item.title: The 2027 COLA Check: Why a Social Security Raise Often Feels Smaller Than It Looks
item.body:
Every fall, millions of Social Security beneficiaries wait for a single percentage: the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. It is meant to help benefits keep pace with rising prices. Yet many retirees open their first statement of the new year and feel the increase has already vanished. This guide explains how the COLA is calculated, why the number on the headline is not the same as the change in your bank deposit, and what to review before January.

*This article is general information, not personal financial, tax, or legal advice. Check the Social Security Administration (SSA) and Medicare for figures that apply to you.*

## How the COLA Is Calculated

The COLA is tied to inflation, but not the version most people see in the news. By law, it is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The basic steps are:

1. The SSA averages the CPI-W for July, August, and September of the current year.
2. It compares that average with the same three-month average from the previous year.
3. The percentage increase, rounded to the nearest tenth of a percent, becomes the COLA.
4. If prices did not rise, there is no COLA. Benefits are not cut in that case.

The new rate is announced in October and applies to benefits starting with the January payment. For people who receive Social Security, the increase shows up in the payment received in January. For Supplemental Security Income (SSI), the higher payment arrives at the start of January.

## Why the Raise Can Feel Smaller

### 1. Medicare Part B premiums are usually deducted first

Most retirees on Medicare pay the Part B premium, and for those who collect Social Security it is typically taken straight out of the monthly benefit. When the premium rises, the net increase shrinks. Part B premiums have climbed in recent years. For reference, the standard monthly premium was $185.00 in 2025 and $202.90 in 2026. The 2027 amount is set by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), so confirm the current figure on Medicare.gov.

A simple example with made-up numbers: a retiree receives $2,000 a month before deductions. A 3% COLA adds $60. If the Part B premium rises by $15 the same month, the real gain is $45, not $60.

### 2. The "hold harmless" rule has limits

A federal protection called the hold harmless provision generally prevents a beneficiary's Social Security check from falling because of a Part B premium increase. But it does not apply to everyone. People who are newly enrolled in Medicare, those who pay higher income-related premiums, and those who do not have the premium deducted from their benefit are generally not covered. It also does not guarantee the COLA will be fully intact, only that the net check will not shrink.

### 3. Higher-income retirees may pay an income-related surcharge

Some beneficiaries pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) on top of the standard Part B and Part D premiums. It is based on tax returns from two years earlier. A raise in benefits, plus other income, can occasionally push someone into a higher bracket.

### 4. Your personal costs may not match CPI-W

CPI-W measures a general basket of goods for working households. Retirees often spend a larger share of income on health care, housing, and utilities. If those categories rise faster than the overall index, a COLA that matches the headline inflation rate can still feel inadequate. Researchers and advocacy groups have long debated whether an index weighted toward older consumers would be more accurate, but the law currently uses CPI-W.

### 5. Taxes can take a bite

Depending on your "combined income" (adjusted gross income, nontaxable interest, and half of your Social Security benefits), up to 85% of your benefit may be subject to federal income tax. The income thresholds are not indexed to inflation. As benefits rise with COLAs over time, more retirees can find a portion of their benefit taxed. Some states also tax benefits, though most do not.

### 6. Other deductions and premiums

Medicare Part D drug plan premiums, Medicare Advantage plan premiums, supplemental (Medigap) policy premiums, and deductibles often change at the start of the year. Not all of these come out of the Social Security check, but they affect your total budget.

## A January Checklist

Use the weeks before the new year to review the details:

- **Find your official notice.** The SSA sends a COLA notice that shows your new gross benefit, the Part B premium withheld, and your net payment. Many people can view it in their online *my Social Security* account.
- **Compare gross and net.** Write down your current deposit and your expected deposit after the Part B premium and any other withholding. This is the number that matters for your monthly budget.
- **Review your Medicare plan during open enrollment.** The annual Medicare open enrollment period runs from October 15 to December 7. Compare drug coverage and Medicare Advantage plans, since premiums, copays, and covered drugs can change.
- **Check for IRMAA letters.** If your income dropped because of retirement or another life event, you may be able to request a new determination from the SSA.
- **Adjust tax withholding.** If a larger share of your benefit becomes taxable, consider whether to update withholding using Form W-4V or make estimated payments, so there is no surprise at tax time.
- **Look at your spending categories.** Track housing, health care, food, and utilities for a few months to see which costs are actually rising for you.
- **Ask about assistance programs.** Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help for prescription costs, and state or local assistance may help people with limited income and resources. Your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) offers free counseling.
- **Beware of scams.** The SSA does not call to demand payment or threaten to suspend your benefit over a COLA. Use official channels such as ssa.gov and be wary of unsolicited calls, texts, or emails.

## The Bottom Line

The COLA is an important protection against inflation, and it adjusts every year without an application. But the headline percentage is a starting point, not the final answer. What lands in your account depends on Medicare premiums, taxes, and how your own expenses compare with the national index. Review your official notice, compare your net deposit with your real costs, and use the fall enrollment season to look for savings. A few hours of checking now can make the January change far less of a surprise.

*Figures and rules can change. Confirm the current COLA, Medicare premiums, and thresholds with the Social Security Administration (ssa.gov) and Medicare (medicare.gov).*
